open-question.question: On a host without a blocking wait, where the orchestrator batches per wake-up, does the dispatch prompt still name a run scratch directory for the agent to write into, so the agent's contract and the prompt are the same on every host, or does the agent choose its own scratch path there and the prompt keep its two values?
open-question.alternative: The orchestrator creates one run scratch directory on every host, including a host without a blocking wait where it batches per wake-up, and passes that directory as a third value in the dispatch prompt beside the Short Title and `<MILESTONE_DIR>`. The dispatch prompt template in `core/skills/provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions/SKILL.md` and the agent file `core/agents/provide-alternatives-to-open-question.md` stay host-neutral and unconditional: the agent writes its one file into the named directory and returns that file's path. No slot is added and no existing slot carries the directory line, so the waiting sentence stays the only part that differs by host. The agent's contract, the prompt, the agent file, and the `CLAUDE.md` dispatch-prompt invariant read the same in every host tree. The per-wake-up form then differs from the single-wait form only in when the orchestrator embeds, which matches the goal's single host slot. Every return lands in one known place per run, so a batch can be assembled the same way on every host. On a per-wake-up host the orchestrator creates and names a directory that it does not need for waiting, which adds one more value it must create and hold for each dispatch. The orchestrator and the agent must both be able to write to the same directory. On Codex, where temp-directory writability under the sandbox is unrecorded, that is not yet established, and it depends on the sibling question about the scratch directory's location. If the sibling Codex and Antigravity wait-form questions give every host the single-wait form, no per-wake-up host is left and this question is moot.

On a host without a blocking wait the dispatch prompt keeps its two values, Short Title and `<MILESTONE_DIR>`. The directory line appears only in the single-wait hosts' prompt, carried by a per-host value such as the existing `ALTERNATIVES_PROMPT_INSTRUCTIONS` prefix slot or the waiting slot's own wording, so no new slot is declared. The one host-neutral agent file states both cases. If the prompt names a scratch directory, the agent writes its file there. Otherwise it creates its own scratch file outside the repository, for example a fresh temporary file, and returns that path. The per-wake-up host's prompt stays exactly two values, so the orchestrator there creates and holds nothing extra. On a sandboxed host the agent picks a location it can actually write to itself, which avoids a shared directory whose writability is unrecorded. The agent's contract is no longer the same on every host. It carries a branch keyed on whether a value is present, and `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/design-claims.md` claim 13, and the skill reference must describe two prompt shapes. On a per-wake-up host the scratch files of one run are scattered, so the orchestrator learns each path only from the returns. That fits only if the sibling question about scratch file naming and return settles on the agent reporting its path. Placing the directory line in an existing per-host slot also stretches what that slot means, and this interacts with the sibling question about where the waiting wording is placed.

alternative.id: Two values, per-host agent contract slot

open-question.alternative: On a host without a blocking wait the dispatch prompt keeps its two values, as in the conditional option. The difference is in the agent file: the sentence saying where the agent writes becomes a new host slot in `core/agents/provide-alternatives-to-open-question.md`, declared by all three host definitions. Each rendered tree's agent file states only its own case: write into the directory the prompt names on a single-wait host, or choose your own scratch file outside the repository on a per-wake-up host. The prompt's directory line rides a matching per-host value. Each host tree's agent reads one unconditional contract with no branch, and the per-wake-up host still creates and passes nothing beyond today's two values. The build's `slot-declaration` check keeps the per-host wording consistent with the three host definitions. It adds a second host slot, which contradicts the goal's statement that the waiting sentence is the one host slot, so choosing it would mean revising the goal. It also splits the agent file, today free of any wording slot, across hosts. If Antigravity is not given the Claude Code value, that split breaks the byte-identity between the Claude Code and Antigravity trees. Like the conditional option, it depends on the sibling question about scratch file naming and return settling on the agent reporting its path, and it is moot if no host ends up with the per-wake-up form.

open-question.question: When the orchestrator creates the run's scratch directory, where outside the repository does it create it: a fresh temporary directory under the system temp location, the host's session scratchpad, or another place, given that temp-directory writability under the Codex sandbox is unrecorded?

Is each agent's scratch file name derived from its Short Title by a fixed rule, so the orchestrator knows every path before any agent returns and the agent's final message can be a bare success token, or does the agent choose its own file name and report the path as its final message, so the orchestrator learns the paths only from the returns?

In the single-wait form, what does the blocking wait test to decide that every dispatched agent has finished, and how does an agent that ends with FAILED and writes no elements become visible to that test: a failure marker it writes beside the other files, a bounded wait that gives up, or the host's own completion signal?

Which Claude Code primitive is the blocking wait: a foreground shell loop inside one tool call under its ten-minute cap, a background shell loop or Monitor that returns at once and notifies later, or something else, given that a foreground sleep ran when tested although the host states foreground sleep is blocked?

What does the orchestrator do when the blocking wait ends before every dispatched agent has finished: embed and commit what has landed and wait again, fall back to per-wake-up batching for the rest, or treat the unfinished agents as skipped?
open-question.alternative: When the blocking wait ends with agents still unfinished, the orchestrator pipes every file that has landed so far into one `embed --alternatives` batch and commits each question that embedded, in one shell call. It then issues the same blocking wait again for the agents still outstanding, and repeats until every dispatched agent has landed a file or ended in a failure. No limit is set on how many times it waits again, nothing is skipped because of an expiry, and the run keeps the single-wait form throughout. Finished work is committed at every expiry, so a slow agent never holds the rest hostage and an interrupted run loses only uncommitted returns. Each expiry adds just one batch-plus-wait turn pair, and the run stays in one waiting form on one host. A hung agent keeps the run waiting forever unless the wait's completion test turns it into a failure some other way (the sibling "Wait completion and failure test" owns that). A run with several expiries also makes several batch calls, so the goal's "wakes once per run" holds only when nothing expires.

alternative.id: Embed landed, wait bounded times, then skip

open-question.alternative: At each expiry the orchestrator embeds and commits every landed file in one shell call, then waits again for the outstanding agents. It does this up to a fixed number of further waits (or a fixed total waiting time). After the last allowed wait it embeds whatever has landed and treats every agent still unfinished as skipped. Those questions are listed in the step-4 still-skipped advisory, and a later run of the pass picks them up because their blocks still carry no alternatives. The run's length is bounded, so a hung or runaway agent cannot stall the pass, and slow but healthy agents still get several chances to land. Committed progress accumulates at every expiry. It adds a tunable bound (a count or a duration) to the prose, and that bound has to be justified per host. An agent skipped at the bound may still finish later and write a file that nothing embeds, wasting its tokens and leaving an orphan in the scratch directory. It also stretches the skip from "refused after repair" to "too slow", which changes what the advisory means.

alternative.id: Hold landed, wait again until all land

open-question.alternative: At an expiry the orchestrator embeds nothing. It just issues the blocking wait again for the outstanding agents, with no limit, so every landed file stays in the scratch directory until the whole set has landed or failed. Then it embeds and commits the whole set in the one batch shell call the goal describes. An expiry is invisible to the batching: the run still makes exactly one embed-and-commit call. It keeps the goal's single-wake, single-batch shape exactly, whatever the host's wait cap. The orchestrator adds no branch, only a repeated wait, which is the smallest change to the waiting sentence. Nothing is committed until the slowest agent finishes, so an orchestrator that dies or is interrupted mid-wait commits none of the landed work, and a re-run re-dispatches every bare block. A hung agent stalls the whole run unless the wait's completion test (owned by the sibling "Wait completion and failure test") ends it some other way.

alternative.id: Hold landed, wait bounded times, then batch and skip

open-question.alternative: At an expiry the orchestrator embeds nothing and waits again, up to a fixed number of further waits (or a fixed total waiting time). When every agent has landed or failed, or the bound is reached, it embeds and commits every landed file in one batch shell call. Any agent still unfinished at the bound is treated as skipped and reported in the step-4 still-skipped advisory, to be picked up by a later run of the pass. It keeps exactly one embed-and-commit call per run and still bounds how long the run can last, so neither a long wait cap nor a hung agent changes the batch shape or stalls the pass forever. Landed work stays uncommitted for the whole bounded window, so an interruption loses all of it. It adds a tunable bound, and skipping slow agents leaves orphan files and wasted agent tokens just as the progressive bounded form does.

alternative.id: Embed landed, switch to per-wake-up batching

open-question.alternative: At the first expiry the orchestrator embeds and commits every landed file in one shell call. It then drops the blocking wait for the rest of the run and handles the outstanding agents the way a host without a blocking wait does: it batches every landed return each time it wakes on the host's own completion signal, until every agent has landed or failed. The single-wait form covers the first window, and the per-wake-up form covers whatever is left after it. It reuses the per-wake-up path the goal already writes for hosts without a blocking wait, so expiry needs no new waiting logic. The orchestrator stops blocking on a tool call it cannot extend, and slow agents are still embedded as they finish. Both waiting forms have to be live and correct on the same host within one run, so the waiting sentence must describe the hand-off between them. It works only where the host also delivers per-agent completion wake-ups, which depends on which primitive the sibling "Claude Code wait primitive" picks and on what the siblings "Codex wait form" and "Antigravity wait form" settle. After the switch the run returns to several wake-ups, some of them turns that do nothing.

When the wait ends early, the orchestrator embeds and commits every landed file in one shell call and treats every agent still unfinished as skipped. It neither waits again nor switches form. The skipped questions are listed in the step-4 still-skipped advisory, and their blocks stay bare, so the next run of the pass dispatches them afresh. It is the simplest rule and keeps the run to exactly one wait and one batch, with a hard ceiling on run time set by the host's wait cap. Recovery is already built in, because the pass's idempotent gather re-selects every bare block on its next run. Any agent slower than one wait cap loses its work every time, so on a host with a short cap (a ten-minute foreground call) a large or slow question can be skipped run after run. Agents still running write files that no one embeds, wasting their tokens, unless the orchestrator also stops them. It also turns "slow" into a skip reason that the existing one-repair-then-skip contract never had.

open-question.question: Does the Codex tree get the single-wait form, waiting on each cap-sized round of agents through Codex's own agent tools, or the per-wake-up value, given its subagent thread cap and that the repository records no Codex waiting tool?

Does the Antigravity tree carry the same waiting sentence as Claude Code, keeping the two trees byte-identical on the assumption that it offers the same wait, or the per-wake-up value, given that the repository records nothing about how Antigravity delivers agent returns?

When a batch call refuses some returns, does the orchestrator send every repair at once and wait for the repaired returns as one further batch, or repair and re-embed each refused return on its own as it comes back?

Which returns does one batch call pipe: only those the wake-up's notifications or the finished wait named, or every file present in the scratch directory, and in the latter case how does the orchestrator avoid re-piping a file it embedded in an earlier batch?

Are the scratch files and their directory deleted by the orchestrator, after each successful embed or at the end of the run, or left in place for the host's temp handling and for inspecting refused returns?

alternative.id: Delete each file after its embed, keep refused files

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator deletes each scratch file in the same shell call as the batch that embedded it, as soon as `embed --alternatives` accepts it. Files that were refused, or that belong to a question still skipped after its repair, stay where they are. At the end of the run the orchestrator removes the run's scratch directory only if it is empty, with a non-recursive remove that does nothing when files remain. Whatever is left is handed to the host's temp handling. Only the files that matter for diagnosis survive: each one is a return the tool refused or a question the end-of-run advisory already names as skipped. Deleting at embed time also means a later batch on a per-wake-up host never finds an already-embedded file in the directory to pipe again. It adds a delete step to every batch and a conditional directory removal to the run's end, all in the prose of the one shell call the goal keeps small. The empty-only removal also leaves a directory behind on every run that skipped a question. It needs the orchestrator to know each file's path at embed time, which depends on the naming and scratch-directory-in-prompt siblings.

alternative.id: Delete each file after its embed, remove the directory at run end

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator deletes each scratch file in the same shell call as the batch that embedded it. At the end of the run it removes the whole scratch directory recursively, including any refused or skipped returns still inside it. Nothing from the run outlives it. The run leaves nothing behind wherever the directory lives, whatever the host's temp policy. Per-embed deletion still keeps a later batch from re-piping an embedded file. The one return worth inspecting is destroyed: a refused or skipped return whose `Error:` line the advisory reports, which was the only evidence of why it failed. It adds deletion prose in two places. A recursive remove of a path the orchestrator built is a risky command to write into a runner, and it may raise a permission prompt in a headless chain where no one can answer it.

alternative.id: Remove the whole directory at run end only

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator leaves every scratch file in place while the run is going. After the last batch, and after the commits and any repairs, it removes the run's scratch directory recursively in one command, refused and skipped returns included. Nothing is deleted per embed. Cleanup is one command at one point in the run, separate from the per-batch embed-and-commit call. In the single-wait form, where there is only one batch, it costs exactly what per-embed deletion costs. Refused returns are lost just as in the per-embed variant. On a per-wake-up host, embedded files stay in the directory between batches, so it only works if the batch-input-selection sibling avoids re-piping them some other way. A run that stops early on a tool failure skips the final removal and leaves everything behind anyway.

alternative.id: At run end, delete embedded files and keep refused ones

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator leaves every scratch file in place while the run is going. After the last batch it deletes the files whose questions embedded and keeps the refused or skipped returns. It removes the directory only if it is empty, otherwise leaving it to the host's temp handling. Like per-embed deletion, it keeps the failed returns for inspection, and it collects all cleanup into one end-of-run step instead of spreading it across batches. To delete selectively at the end, the orchestrator has to carry the embedded/refused split through the whole run, which is extra state for an orchestrator meant to hold no work context. On a per-wake-up host, embedded files stay in the directory between batches, so it relies on the batch-input-selection sibling to avoid re-piping them. An early stop leaves everything behind.

alternative.id: No deletion, leave it to host temp handling

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator deletes nothing: no scratch file, no directory, at no point in the run. The run's scratch directory and every return in it, embedded or refused, are left to the host's own temp handling. That could be system temp cleanup or the expiry of the session scratchpad. It is the least runner prose and the fewest commands, with no remove command to word safely or to get a permission prompt in a headless chain. Every return, accepted or refused, can be inspected after the run, the same way the transcripts were mined for the token report. Files pile up across runs at a rate that depends entirely on where the directory lives (the scratch-directory-location sibling), and nothing in the repository records Codex's or Antigravity's temp handling. Copies of milestone content sit outside the repository until something else clears them. On a per-wake-up host, embedded files stay in the directory, so it relies on the batch-input-selection sibling, and on a fresh directory per run, to avoid re-piping a file it already embedded.

open-question.question: Does the waiting wording live in the existing ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY slot, whose values already say how returns are handled as they land, or in a new slot of its own, with the concurrency slot left to say only how many dispatches run at once?
